newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Record prize money at next world chess championship.
newsitem.headline: Record prize money at next world chess championship.

text.p: The World Chess federation (FIDE) said on Tuesday it would offer record prize money for its next world championship, which would be run under a new system to make it more spectacular and prestigious.
There would be a prize fund of five million dollars, the largest ever offered in a chess championship, said FIDE President Kirsan Ilyumzhinov.
The money would be shared proportionately between all the participants, with $1,370,000 for the winner.

Ilyumzhinov, who is also president of the republic of Kalmykia in southern Russia, said he hoped to attract leading grandmaster Garry Kasparov to the championship, due to start at the end of the year.
"I want to distance chess from the political wranglings which it is caught up in and so we had to carry out a revolution in chess," Ilyumzhinov told a news conference.
Kasparov, who split with FIDE in 1993 to set up his own rival championship, the Professional Chess Association (PCA), has up to now ruled out returning to the FIDE fold.
But Ilyumzhinov hopes PCA champion Kasparov will take on archrival and FIDE title-holder Anatoly Karpov in the next FIDE contest.
"We are sending invitations to Garry Kasparov and Anatoly Karpov to take part in the championship," said Ilyumzhinov, adding that they would be allowed to join from the semi-finals.
FIDE said the competition would be held on December 16, 1997 to January 8, 1998, in Elista, capital of the Kalmyk republic, and aim to involve one hundred competitors playing eight rounds.
"The Olympic system (the looser leaves) and compressed time-frames will make this competition a really fascinating one," a FIDE statement said.
Previous FIDE competitions, held over three years and involving regional and inter-regional tournaments, were no longer appropriate today when sponsorship was key, it said.
The semi-finals would consist of six games and the finals of either four or eight, Ilyumzhinov said.
He told Reuters that he hoped the new rules would lure Kasparov to the tournament. "I am eager to end long-standing rivalries and create conditions for them to play."
